questions.q: The word 'agriculture' comes from Latin. What does the part 'agri' mean?
questions.a: Field: agri means field and culture means to cultivate.

questions.q: The chapter says that, very broadly, agriculture covers farming, animal husbandry, forestry and horticulture. What does 'animal husbandry' mean?
questions.a: Raising livestock: the chapter explains animal husbandry in brackets as raising livestock.

questions.q: True or False: The chapter describes farming as one of the newest occupations of humankind. Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says farming or agriculture is one of the oldest occupations of humankind.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: farming is one of the oldest occupations of humankind

questions.q: Answer briefly from the chapter: (a) What is pisciculture? (b) What is another name for beekeeping? (c) What is threshing?
questions.a: (a) Pisciculture is fish rearing. (b) Apiculture. (c) Threshing is removing the edible grain from the straw or husk, by hand or using a machine.
s: Pisciculture: fish rearing
Beekeeping is also called apiculture
Threshing: removing the edible grain from the straw or husk, manually or by machine

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. Fibre production, such as cotton and hemp, is left out of 'agriculture and allied activities', because fibres are not food.
II. Very broadly, the term agriculture covers farming, animal husbandry, forestry and horticulture.
III. The chapter gives the saffron valley of Kashmir and the tea gardens of the Nilgiris as examples of India's varied agriculture.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: the Government of India's 'agriculture and allied activities' includes fibre production such as cotton and hemp, along with livestock, beekeeping, fisheries and silkworm rearing; being food is not the test.

questions.q:
During her holidays, Mitali stayed on her grandmother's farm near Jorhat in Assam. Her diary lists one week's work. Monday: the women of the family transplanted paddy seedlings. Tuesday: her uncle fed the silkworms on the cocoon racks. Wednesday: the family fed the fish in their pond and netted some for sale. Thursday: two areca nut saplings were planted along the field edge. Friday: the paddy from the small upper field was beaten to separate the grain from the straw.
(a) Which day's work is pisciculture?
(b) What is the name for Friday's work?
(c) What is Tuesday's work done for, and does the Government of India count it under 'agriculture and allied activities'?
(d) A visitor's leaflet about the farm says, 'The farmer here is Mitali's uncle; he does the farm work.' Using Monday's entry and the chapter's figure for rural India, explain why the leaflet's picture of a farmer is probably wrong, and name two other farm operations the chapter says women perform.
questions.a: (a) Wednesday: rearing fish in the pond is pisciculture. (b) Threshing: removing the edible grain from the straw or husk. (c) Rearing silkworms is done to get cocoons from which silk thread is extracted; yes, the government includes rearing silkworms and preparing silk yarn in agriculture and allied activities. (d) On Monday the women of the family did the transplanting. The chapter says many people imagine a man when they hear 'farmer', but in rural India more than 75 per cent of people working in agriculture are women (2025), and they perform most farming operations, such as sowing, harvesting and threshing. So the farm work is probably done mostly by women, not by the uncle alone.
s: (a) Wednesday: fish rearing in the pond is pisciculture
(b) Friday's work is threshing
(c) Silkworms are reared for cocoons that give silk thread; yes, silkworm rearing is an allied activity
(d) Uses Monday's entry and the figure of more than 75 per cent women in rural agriculture to reject the leaflet, naming two operations such as sowing and harvesting

questions.q: Answer in five short parts about India's agricultural landscape. (a) Give the meaning of the two Latin parts of the word 'agriculture'. (b) Name the four broad fields the term agriculture covers. (c) About what share of India's gross domestic product came from agriculture and allied activities in 2022-23? (d) About what share of India's working population depended on agriculture and allied activities in 2022-23? (e) Name two places the chapter gives as examples of India's varied farming, with the crop or plantation of each.
questions.a: (a) Agri means field and culture means to cultivate. (b) Farming, animal husbandry (raising livestock), forestry and horticulture. (c) A little over 18 per cent. (d) About 46 per cent. (e) Any two of: wheat fields of Punjab, saffron valley of Kashmir, tea gardens of the Northeast or the Nilgiris, paddy fields of Kerala.
s: (a) Agri = field, culture = to cultivate
(b) Farming, animal husbandry, forestry and horticulture
(c) A little over 18 per cent of GDP
(d) About 46 per cent of the working population
(e) Two place-crop pairs such as Punjab wheat and Kashmir saffron

questions.q: The Vedas mention a crop called godhuma. Which crop is it?
questions.a: Wheat: the Vedas name yava (barley), godhuma (wheat) and vrihi (rice).

questions.q: Which of these correctly describes intercropping?
o: Growing two or more different crops in the same field at the same time
Growing different crops in the same field in different seasons
Growing the same single crop in a field year after year
Joining one plant with another so they grow as a single plant
questions.a: Growing two or more different crops at the same time; growing them in different seasons is crop rotation, and joining two plants into one is grafting.

questions.q: (a) At which site, in Baluchistan, is the cultivation of barley and millets dated to the 7th millennium BCE? (b) Name the two staple crops of the Harappans.
questions.a: (a) Mehrgarh. (b) Barley and wheat.
s: (a) Mehrgarh
(b) Barley and wheat

questions.q:
Match each ancient text in Column A with the person or people linked to it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Arthashastra  2. Brihatsamhita  3. Vrikshayurveda  4. Sangam literature
Column B: (p) Surapala  (q) the early Tamils  (r) Kautilya  (s) Varahamihira
questions.a: 1-r, 2-s, 3-p, 4-q: Kautilya's Arthashastra, Varahamihira's Brihatsamhita, Surapala's Vrikshayurveda and the Sangam literature of the early Tamils.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Surapala's Vrikshayurveda is a useful source for anyone studying how ancient Indian farmers prepared seeds and planted crops.
Reason (R): The Vrikshayurveda gives recommendations on seed preparation, soil cultivation methods and planting techniques.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the text is useful for studying seed preparation and planting because, as the chapter says, it gives recommendations on exactly these, along with soil cultivation methods.

questions.q: Kunal says, 'Ancient Indian texts on agriculture dealt only with field crops; they said nothing about animals or trees.' Is he right? Give your verdict and two pieces of evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says some ancient texts also refer to the rearing and care of animals. The texts also contain writings on horticulture and plant biodiversity: Surapala's Vrikshayurveda advises watering newly planted trees in arid land every morning and evening for fifteen days, and the Brihatsamhita describes a method of grafting still used today.
s: Verdict: No, the claim is wrong
Evidence on animals: some texts refer to the rearing and care of animals
Evidence on trees: Vrikshayurveda's advice on watering newly planted trees, or the Brihatsamhita's grafting method, or writings on horticulture

questions.q: At a heritage seed fair, a stall shows eight seeds: safflower, linseed, black gram, fenugreek, hemp, jute, jujube and black plum. Its banner says, 'All these were grown by the first farmers of Mehrgarh, long before any animal was domesticated.' (a) Using the chapter's groups, which two seeds are oilseeds and which two are legumes? (b) Which two are fibre crops and which two are fruits? (c) What does the chapter say was cultivated at Mehrgarh in the 7th millennium BCE, and why does this not support the banner's first claim? (d) Name two animals domesticated from the pre-urban phase of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation (c. 3500 BCE). Then work out at least how many years separate the end of the 7th millennium BCE from c. 3500 BCE.
questions.a: (a) Oilseeds: safflower and linseed. Legumes: black gram and fenugreek. (b) Fibre crops: hemp and jute. Fruits: jujube and black plum. (c) Barley and millets. The chapter says farmers learned to grow oilseeds, legumes, fibre crops and fruits only 'over time', after these early crops, so the eight seeds are not shown at Mehrgarh. (d) Any two of cattle, asses, sheep, goats, dogs, pigs and fowl. The 7th millennium BCE runs from 7000 to 6001 BCE, so its end is 6001 BCE; 6001 - 3500 = 2,501, so at least about 2,500 years.
s: (a) Oilseeds safflower and linseed; legumes black gram and fenugreek
(b) Fibre crops hemp and jute; fruits jujube and black plum
(c) Barley and millets at Mehrgarh; the other groups came 'over time', so the banner is not supported
(d) Two domesticated animals and a gap of at least about 2,500 years (6001 - 3500)

questions.q: During which months does the southwest monsoon bring rain to India?
questions.a: June to September; October to December is the period of the northeast monsoon.

questions.q: Which climate type does the chapter give for the Himalayas?
questions.a: Alpine. Temperate is the lower Himalayas, arid the Thar Desert and tropical wet the western coastal strip.

questions.q: (a) Which factors are combined to create India's agroclimatic zones? (b) Into how many agroclimatic zones is India divided? Name one of them.
questions.a: (a) Climate factors, the types of soil and terrain, and the types of vegetation. (b) 15 zones; for example, the Upper Gangetic Plain Region, the Southern Plateau and Hills Region or the Western Dry Region.
s: (a) Climate, soil and terrain, and vegetation
(b) 15, with one named zone such as the Upper Gangetic Plain Region

questions.q: Answer from the chapter: (a) In which months does the northeast monsoon prevail? (b) To which parts of India does it bring rain? (c) Name the two coastal plains that receive rain from both the southwest and the northeast monsoons.
questions.a: (a) October to December. (b) The east and south of India. (c) The Malabar plain (Kerala) and the Coromandel plain (Tamil Nadu).
s: (a) October to December
(b) East and south India
(c) Malabar (Kerala) and Coromandel (Tamil Nadu) plains

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Dividing India into agroclimatic zones is useful to the government and other agencies that want to improve agricultural production.
Reason (R): The zones help them identify and plan what, when and how to grow different crops.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the chapter says the categorisation helps the government and other agencies identify and plan actions to improve agricultural production, that is, what, when and how to grow crops.

questions.q: A seed scientist has four trial farms: one in the Thar Desert, one on the central Deccan Plateau, one on the western coastal strip and one in the lower Himalayas. She wants to test a millet on the farm with a semi-arid climate. Going by the chapter's list of India's climate types, which farm should she use?
o: The farm on the central Deccan Plateau
The farm in the Thar Desert
The farm on the western coastal strip
The farm in the lower Himalayas
questions.a: The farm on the central Deccan Plateau: the chapter lists the central Deccan Plateau as semi-arid; the Thar Desert is arid, the western coastal strip is tropical wet and the lower Himalayas are temperate.

questions.q: Meenakshi farms on the Coromandel plain in Tamil Nadu. Gurpreet farms near Meerut in western Uttar Pradesh, in the northern plains. Use only the monsoon months given in the chapter, and count each month of a monsoon period as one month of monsoon rain. (a) For how many months of the year does each farmer get monsoon rain? (b) For how many months is each without monsoon rain? (c) Name the climate type the chapter gives for each farmer's region. (d) Of the chapter's three example agroclimatic zones (Upper Gangetic Plain Region, Southern Plateau and Hills Region, Western Dry Region), which one could Gurpreet's farm fall in? Give a reason, and say why the Western Dry Region does not fit.
questions.a: (a) Meenakshi: southwest monsoon June-September (4 months) plus northeast monsoon October-December (3 months) = 7 months. Gurpreet: only the southwest monsoon, 4 months. (b) Meenakshi 12 - 7 = 5 months; Gurpreet 12 - 4 = 8 months. (c) Meenakshi: tropical (eastern India and the southern peninsula); Gurpreet: subtropical (the northern plains). (d) The Upper Gangetic Plain Region: his farm is on the northern plains of the Ganga system, not on the southern plateau. The Western Dry Region names a dry region, like the arid Thar Desert, while his region is subtropical and gets four months of monsoon rain.
s: (a) Meenakshi 7 months (4 + 3); Gurpreet 4 months
(b) Meenakshi 5 months; Gurpreet 8 months without monsoon rain
(c) Meenakshi tropical; Gurpreet subtropical
(d) Upper Gangetic Plain Region with a reason, and the Western Dry Region rejected as a dry region unlike his subtropical plain

questions.q: Which of these is a zaid crop?
questions.a: Watermelon, a summer crop; wheat and mustard are rabi crops and bajra is a kharif crop.

questions.q: According to the chapter's chart of cropping seasons, in what kind of weather are rabi crops grown?
o: The hot summer between rabi and kharif
questions.a: Cool weather with less water: rabi crops are winter crops; hot weather with heavy rainfall is the kharif season.

questions.q:
Match each description in Column A with the term in Column B.
Column A: 1. Seed sown when the monsoon arrives, in hot weather with heavy rain  2. Seed sown in cool weather with less water, a winter crop  3. A crop such as muskmelon grown in the summer season  4. The older name meaning 'wet crops', used before the Arabic terms spread
Column B: (p) zaid  (q) kharif  (r) kedara  (s) rabi
questions.a: 1-q, 2-s, 3-p, 4-r: kharif crops are monsoon crops, rabi crops winter crops, zaid crops summer crops, and kedara was the older name for wet crops.

questions.q: True or False: The terms kharif, rabi and zaid are Sanskrit words that were first used in the Vedas. Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. The terms kharif, rabi and zaid are of Arabic origin and have been in use since Mughal times; before them the seasons' crops were called kedara, haimana and graishmika.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the terms are of Arabic origin, in use since Mughal times

questions.q: (a) Name two kharif crops. (b) State one challenge the chapter says farmers face in the kharif season.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: rice, maize, jowar, bajra, sugarcane, groundnut, cotton. (b) Kharif crops depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon; also, excessive rainfall can destroy the crops.
s: (a) Two kharif crops such as rice and cotton
(b) One challenge: dependence on the timely monsoon, or crop destruction by excessive rain

questions.q: A Class 7 wall chart lists: 'Mustard - kharif', 'Maize - rabi', 'Pumpkin - zaid'. Check each entry. Correct any that are wrong, and for each crop give the weather of its correct season.
questions.a: Mustard is wrong: it is a rabi crop, grown in cool weather with less water. Maize is wrong: it is a kharif crop, grown in hot weather with heavy rainfall. Pumpkin is correct: it is a zaid (summer) crop.
s: Mustard corrected to rabi, with cool weather and less water
Maize corrected to kharif, with hot weather and heavy rainfall
Pumpkin kept as zaid, a summer crop

questions.q:
Saanvi's school in Uttar Pradesh runs a farm-calendar project. She notes her uncle's year. In July he sowed maize and groundnut on his main field. In November he sowed peas and gram on the same field. In March he sowed muskmelon and cucumber on a small plot near the tubewell.
(a) To which cropping season do the July crops belong?
(b) To which season do peas and gram belong, and what is the weather of that season?
(c) To which season do muskmelon and cucumber belong?
(d) Why would her uncle choose the plot near the tubewell for his March crops? Use what the chapter says about that season and about where farmers in north India get water in the dry period.
questions.a: (a) Kharif (monsoon crops). (b) Rabi, the winter crops, grown in cool weather with less water. (c) Zaid, the summer crops. (d) Muskmelon and cucumber are zaid crops, grown in the hot summer season between rabi and kharif, when there is no monsoon rain; farmers in north India then depend on other sources such as groundwater, so a plot next to the tubewell can be watered easily.
s: (a) Kharif
(b) Rabi, cool weather with less water
(c) Zaid
(d) Zaid crops grow in the dry summer without monsoon rain, so they need groundwater from the tubewell

questions.q: Kiran has one field and must choose between two plans for the year. Plan P: monsoon season - wheat; winter - rice; summer - muskmelon. Plan Q: monsoon season - jowar; winter - peas; summer - pumpkin. (a) Which plan matches the chapter's cropping seasons? Name the season of each of its three crops. (b) Find the two mistakes in Plan P and give the weather each wrongly placed crop actually needs. (c) Kiran has no jowar seed but has bajra (pearl millet). Can bajra take jowar's place in Plan Q? Give the reason. (d) Plan P's muskmelon slot is right. Give its season and the older name for crops of that season. (e) Kiran can afford irrigation for only one season. Using the weather the chapter gives for the seasons, which crop of Plan Q is least likely to need it, and why?
questions.a: (a) Plan Q: jowar is a kharif crop, peas a rabi crop and pumpkin a zaid crop. (b) Wheat is placed in the monsoon but is a rabi crop, grown in cool weather with less water; rice is placed in winter but is a kharif crop, sown with the monsoon in hot weather with heavy rainfall. (c) Yes: bajra, like jowar, is a kharif (monsoon) crop. (d) Zaid, the summer crops; they were earlier called graishmika. (e) Jowar, the kharif crop: it grows in the monsoon season of hot weather and heavy rainfall, while peas grow in cool weather with less water and pumpkin in the summer season without the monsoon.
s: (a) Plan Q, with jowar kharif, peas rabi, pumpkin zaid
(b) Wheat is rabi (cool, less water) and rice is kharif (hot, heavy rainfall)
(c) Yes, bajra is also a kharif crop
(d) Zaid (summer crops), earlier called graishmika
(e) Jowar, because the kharif season has heavy monsoon rain

questions.q: Which soil of India is also called cotton soil?
questions.a: Black soil, formed by the weathering of volcanic rocks; laterite soil is the one also called brick earth.

questions.q: Which of these describes humus?
o: Dark organic matter formed by the decomposition of plant and animal matter
Fine rock particles carried by rivers from the mountains to the plains
The original rock from which new rocks and soils are derived
A chemical that turns soil reddish when it reacts with air and water
questions.a: Dark organic matter formed by the decomposition of plant and animal matter; it is rich in nutrients and retains moisture. The other options describe silt, bedrock and iron.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. The Amarakosha describes twelve types of agricultural land based on soil fertility.
II. Today the soils of India are classified into six major types.
III. Alpine soil is thick, smooth and very fertile.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: alpine soil, formed by the freezing and melting of ice, is thin, rough and rocky.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Black soil holds a lot of moisture and is very fertile.
Reason (R): Black soil is formed from silt brought down by rivers from the mountains.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true but R is false: black soil is formed by the weathering of volcanic rocks; soil made of silt deposits brought by rivers is alluvial soil.

questions.q: (a) What is weathering? (b) Name the three means by which it can take place.
questions.a: (a) Weathering is the process by which rocks and minerals are broken down into soil particles. (b) Physical, chemical or biological means.
s: (a) Rocks and minerals broken down into soil particles
(b) Physical, chemical and biological means

questions.q: Three soils are all formed by weathering, but in different ways. For each soil, state what is weathered or what causes the weathering, and one property of the soil that results. (a) Alpine soil (b) Laterite soil (c) Black soil
questions.a: (a) Alpine soil: rock is weathered by the freezing and melting of ice; the soil is thin, rough and rocky. (b) Laterite soil: rock is weathered by rain, which washes most minerals away; it becomes hard in hot weather, is reddish from iron and aluminium, and is not fertile. (c) Black soil: volcanic rocks are weathered; it holds a lot of moisture and is very fertile.
s: (a) Alpine: freezing and melting of ice; thin, rough and rocky
(b) Laterite: weathering by rain; hardens in heat or is not fertile
(c) Black: weathered volcanic rock; holds moisture and is very fertile

questions.q:
For a geography project, three students bring soil samples from their grandparents' villages and describe them. Card 1, from near Bikaner in Rajasthan: mostly small grains of sand with only a little organic matter. Card 2, from a riverbank village near Kanpur: fine, dust-like mud and sand left by the river in flood. Card 3, from a hill farm in Kerala: reddish soil that sets hard like brick in the hot season and has few minerals left.
(a) Name the soil type on each card.
(b) Which card's soil was carried to its place from somewhere else, rather than formed from the rock beneath it? Explain from how it forms.
(c) Why is the Card 3 soil reddish?
(d) A fourth student can farm only one of the three plots and wants the best harvest of ordinary food crops. Which card's plot should she choose? Justify by comparing all three soils as the chapter describes them.
questions.a: (a) Card 1: sandy (desert) soil; Card 2: alluvial soil; Card 3: laterite soil (brick earth). (b) Card 2: alluvial soil is made of silt deposits (mud, sand and fine particles) brought by rivers from the mountains and plateaus and left on the plains, so it was carried there. (c) In laterite soil most minerals are washed away by rain, leaving largely iron and aluminium, which react with air and water and give a reddish colour. (d) Card 2: alluvial soil is rich in nutrients, while laterite soil (Card 3) is not fertile because its minerals are washed away, and sandy soil (Card 1) is mostly sand grains with only a little organic matter.
s: (a) Sandy or desert soil, alluvial soil, laterite soil
(b) Card 2: alluvial silt brought by rivers from mountains and plateaus
(c) Minerals washed away; iron and aluminium left react with air and water to give a red colour
(d) Chooses Card 2 (rich in nutrients) and rejects laterite (not fertile) and sandy soil (mostly sand, little organic matter)

questions.q: Explain why the chapter calls soil 'the foundation of cultivation'. (a) Define soil. (b) Name the three things soil provides for crops. (c) What is humus, and what two benefits does it give the soil? (d) Using how soil forms, explain why soil lost from a field cannot be quickly replaced. (e) What does the Amarakosha's list of twelve types of agricultural land show about people's knowledge of soil long ago?
questions.a: (a) Soil is the thin, upper layer of the Earth's crust that supports plant life. (b) Nutrients, water and support for crops to grow. (c) Humus is the dark organic matter formed by the decomposition of plant and animal matter; it is rich in nutrients and retains moisture in the soil. (d) Soil forms through the breakdown of rocks and the decay of organic matter, a process lasting from a century to several millennia (over millions of years in all), so lost soil cannot be rebuilt in a few seasons. (e) It shows that people long ago already sorted agricultural land by soil fertility, knowing that soils differ in what they can grow.
s: (a) Thin upper layer of the Earth's crust that supports plant life
(b) Nutrients, water and support
(c) Humus: decomposed plant and animal matter; rich in nutrients and retains moisture
(d) Formation by rock breakdown and decay takes a century to millennia, so soil cannot be quickly replaced
(e) Twelve types by fertility shows early awareness of differences in soil fertility

questions.q: Panchagavya is a fermented mixture of how many cow products?
questions.a: Five: dung, urine, milk, curd and ghee.

questions.q: On a steep hillside, Tenzing cuts flat steps into the slope to farm on. His neighbour, on a gentle slope, ploughs along the natural curves of the hill. Which pair names their methods correctly?
questions.a: Tenzing uses terracing (flat steps that slow water runoff) and the neighbour uses contour ploughing (ploughing along the natural curves of the slope); both reduce soil erosion.

questions.q: Raju plants a row of trees along his field to stop soil erosion, and after each harvest he ploughs the crop residue back into the soil. True or False: Raju is using one contemporary approach to soil conservation and one traditional method that farmers still practise today. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Planting trees (afforestation) is listed among the contemporary approaches that help prevent soil erosion, while ploughing back crop residue is one of the traditional methods the chapter says farmers still practise today.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: afforestation is a contemporary approach; ploughing back crop residue is a traditional method still practised

questions.q: (a) What is soil conservation? (b) Name two kinds of organisms found in healthy soil, and say what they do for it.
questions.a: (a) Soil conservation is the practice of managing soil to prevent its degradation and preserve its productivity. (b) Any two of bacteria, fungi, earthworms and insects; they break down organic material and improve the health of the soil so it can sustain healthy plants.
s: (a) Managing soil to prevent degradation and preserve productivity
(b) Two organisms such as bacteria and earthworms, which break down organic matter and improve soil health

questions.q: (a) What is rain-fed agriculture? (b) What is irrigated agriculture? (c) Name one traditional irrigation system from the chapter and the part of India where it is practised.
questions.a: (a) Farming that relies entirely on rainfall. (b) Farming that uses artificial methods to supply water to crops. (c) Phad systems in Maharashtra, or bamboo drip irrigation in parts of northeastern India.
s: (a) Relies entirely on rainfall
(b) Water supplied to crops by artificial methods
(c) Phad systems (Maharashtra) or bamboo drip irrigation (northeast India)

questions.q:
Match each irrigation method in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Drip irrigation  2. Sprinkler irrigation  3. Phad system  4. Bamboo drip irrigation
Column B: (p) sprays water into the air so that it falls on crops like rain  (q) a community system using small canals to divert river water to fields  (r) pipes made of bamboo carry water from springs to fields  (s) water reaches the roots slowly through a network of tubes and emitters
questions.a: 1-s, 2-p, 3-q, 4-r: drip irrigation feeds the roots through tubes and emitters, sprinklers spray water like rain, phad systems divert river water by small canals, and bamboo drip irrigation channels spring water through bamboo pipes.

questions.q: The Thomas family grows paddy on flat land in Kerala. They face three problems: (1) strong winds sweep across the open fields and loosen soil along the bunds, and they would like one more crop from the same land; (2) they spread chemical fertiliser by guesswork, and much of it is wasted; (3) their crops often fall ill, and they want a natural mixture that acts as a biofertiliser. For each problem, recommend one practice from the chapter and explain how it helps. Then judge whether the family should use only traditional practices or combine them with contemporary ones.
questions.a: (1) Grow banana trees on the bunds of the paddy fields: the chapter shows such trees serving as windbreakers, holding the soil in place and giving the farmers another crop. (2) Very precise application of fertilisers: it allows their efficient use and also maintains soil health. (3) Panchagavya, a fermented mixture of five cow products (dung, urine, milk, curd and ghee): studies show it acts as a biofertiliser, enhancing crop growth and productivity and increasing resistance to diseases. Judgement: combine them. Panchagavya is a traditional preparation now supported by recent studies, while precise application of fertilisers is a contemporary approach; using both meets all three problems.
s: (1) Banana trees on bunds: windbreak, hold soil, extra crop
(2) Very precise application of fertilisers: efficient use, maintains soil health
(3) Panchagavya: five cow products, a biofertiliser that improves growth and disease resistance
Judgement to combine traditional and contemporary practices, with a reason

questions.q: Answer in five short parts about caring for soil and water. (a) Name two traditional soil conservation methods. (b) Name two contemporary soil conservation methods. (c) Name two ways in which rain-fed farmers have adapted to droughts and unpredictable monsoons. (d) Write any four names from the chapter's vocabulary of traditional water structures. (e) State one way in which modern irrigation has helped India's agriculture.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: crop rotation, multiple cropping, contour ploughing, organic fertilisers such as cow dung, mulching, ploughing back crop residue (the chapter calls the last two traditional methods still practised today). (b) Any two of: terracing, afforestation, very precise application of fertilisers; mulching or ploughing back crop residue is also accepted here, as the chapter lists them under contemporary approaches as traditional methods still in use, but the same method earns credit in only one of (a) and (b). (c) Choosing drought-resistant crops and using traditional water-harvesting techniques. (d) Any four of: kull, kund, ahar, pokhar, khadin, arakere, kolam, surangam, tadagam, eri. (e) Any one of: farming became possible even in low-rainfall areas; crop yields increased; food supply became more stable; water is used more efficiently.
s: (a) Two traditional methods such as crop rotation, contour ploughing, mulching or ploughing back crop residue
(b) Two contemporary methods such as terracing and afforestation (mulching or ploughing back residue also accepted if not used in (a))
(c) Drought-resistant crops and traditional water harvesting
(d) Four water-structure names such as kull, kund, ahar and eri
(e) One benefit such as farming in low-rainfall areas or higher yields

questions.q: Which state became the world's first 100 per cent organic state?
questions.a: Sikkim, which banned chemical fertilisers and pesticides in 2014.

questions.q: Anil follows traditional agriculture, which treats the plant and the soil as one complete system. His son asks what the soil's bacteria and fungi and his crop do for each other. Which answer fits the chapter?
o: The bacteria and fungi turn soil nutrients into forms the plant can take up; the plant supplies them energy through its roots
The plant turns soil nutrients into forms the bacteria can use; the bacteria and fungi supply the plant energy through its roots
The bacteria and fungi supply the plant with farmyard manure; the plant gives them shade from its leaves
The bacteria and fungi feed on the plant's roots, so the farmer must remove them for a good crop
questions.a: The bacteria and fungi turn soil nutrients into forms the plant can easily take up, and the plant supports them by supplying energy through its roots; the other choices reverse the roles or treat the organisms as pests.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): More and more agricultural scientists the world over question the sustainability of Green Revolution-type farming.
Reason (R): The Green Revolution led to a significant increase in food grain production, particularly of wheat and rice.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A: R is a success of the Green Revolution, while scientists question it because of its limits, such as soil impoverishment, groundwater depletion and contamination by pesticides and fertilisers.

questions.q: (a) Which three operations did the ancient Indian seed drill combine? (b) What was the benefit of combining them?
questions.a: (a) Soil preparation, seed planting and the closing of the furrow. (b) Doing them in one operation reduced the labour of what would have been a three-step operation.
s: (a) Soil preparation, seed planting and closing the furrow
(b) One operation instead of three, reducing labour

questions.q: True or False: ICAR tested every one of the almost 5,000 traditional farming practices it documented. Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. ICAR documented almost 5,000 traditional practices but tested over a hundred of them; over 85 per cent of those were validated by modern science.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: almost 5,000 documented, over a hundred tested, over 85 per cent validated

questions.q: The chapter says that a trade-off is evident when traditional and modern farming methods are compared. Explain this trade-off: give one strength and one weakness of modern (Green Revolution) methods, one strength and one weakness of traditional methods, and the challenge the chapter sets for today.
questions.a: Modern methods are highly productive and can produce a large amount of food quickly, but their chemicals pollute water sources and harm creatures like bees needed for pollination. Traditional methods are often more resilient and sustainable because they work in harmony with Nature, but they may yield lower results. The challenge is to find a balance: use modern innovations to meet food needs while adopting the sustainable practices of our ancestors.
s: Modern: highly productive, but chemicals pollute water or harm bees
Traditional: resilient and sustainable, but may give lower yields
Challenge: balance both, meeting food needs with sustainable practices

questions.q:
The Reddy family in Telangana keeps farm records (figures invented for this question). In 1965 their rice field gave 1.5 tonnes per hectare, grown with saved seed and cow dung. Around 1972 they began using high-yielding seed, canal water, chemical fertiliser and pesticide, and the yield reached 3.6 tonnes per hectare. By 2020 the yield had slipped to 3.0 tonnes, their borewell had to be deepened from 30 m to 90 m, and bees were rarely seen near the field.
(a) The 1972 changes match which movement? Name two of its features seen in the record.
(b) By what percentage did the yield rise from 1965 to 1972?
(c) Which two limits of these methods named in the chapter do the 2020 records show?
(d) The family is thinking of switching to organic farming, as Sikkim did. Give one likely gain and one likely risk, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Green Revolution of the 1960s and 1970s; features seen: high-yielding varieties of seeds, increased irrigation, chemical fertilisers and pesticides (any two). (b) (3.6 - 1.5) / 1.5 x 100 = 140 per cent. (c) Depletion of groundwater (the borewell had to go three times deeper) and long-term impoverishment of the soil (falling yield); the missing bees also fit the harm chemicals do to bees needed for pollination. (d) Gain: organic farming avoids chemical fertilisers and pesticides, so it protects water, soil and creatures such as bees. Risk: traditional, nature-friendly methods may give lower yields, so the family's harvest could fall.
s: (a) Green Revolution, with two features such as HYV seeds and chemical fertilisers
(b) Rise of 140 per cent, from (3.6 - 1.5) / 1.5
(c) Groundwater depletion and soil impoverishment (or harm to bees)
(d) One gain such as protecting soil, water and bees, and one risk such as lower yields

questions.q: Analyse the 'sustainable pathways' the chapter describes. (a) What does organic farming avoid, and name three natural fertilisers it relies on. (b) Why are neem-based pesticides preferred to chemical ones? (c) Sustainable agriculture is inspired by Indian Knowledge Systems. What does it try to combine, and what kind of farming practices does it focus on? (d) Name the three agricultural heritage systems in India that the FAO has recognised. (e) Which of the three combines crop plantation with fishing, and how does it show the chapter's idea of combining farming activities rather than growing one crop?
questions.a: (a) Organic farming avoids chemical fertilisers and pesticides and relies on compost, seed cake (the residue left after oil is extracted from seeds) and manure from animal sources. (b) They are natural and much less harmful to the environment than chemical ones. (c) It combines the productivity of modern methods with the wisdom of traditional practices, and focuses on environment-friendly, long-lasting farming practices. (d) The farming of saffron in Kashmir, the traditional agricultural systems of Odisha that integrate forest management, and the below-sea-level agricultural methods of Kerala. (e) The Kerala system: it integrates paddy farming in saline water with fishing and rearing livestock on the same land, instead of depending on a single crop.
s: (a) Avoids chemical fertilisers and pesticides; compost, seed cake and animal manure
(b) Neem pesticides are natural and much less harmful to the environment
(c) Combines modern productivity with traditional wisdom; environment-friendly, long-lasting practices
(d) Kashmir saffron, Odisha forest-integrated systems, Kerala below-sea-level farming
(e) Kerala: paddy with fishing and livestock, an integrated system

questions.q: The chapter compares India's average landholding of about three-fourths of a hectare with the size of:
o: A large city park of many hectares
questions.a: An average football field.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. Of late, machines have been designed and invented for small farms too.
II. The Ganga river is still able to replenish itself fully, and all of it stays navigable in summer.
III. According to some estimates, as many as 2,300 farmers every day are compelled to abandon agriculture.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the Ganga is increasingly unable to replenish itself, and parts of it are no longer navigable in summer because the water level is too low even for river boats.

questions.q: A residents' group in Chennai wants to grow vegetables on a building terrace that has no garden soil. (a) Which method from the chapter lets them grow plants without soil, and how do the plants get their minerals? (b) Why does the chapter say this method suits such a place?
questions.a: (a) Hydroponics: plants are grown in nutrient-rich water solutions, and essential minerals are given directly to the roots. (b) It is used in controlled environments, which makes it an option for urban farming and for areas with poor soil quality.
s: (a) Hydroponics, with minerals given directly to the roots in nutrient-rich water
(b) It works in controlled environments, suiting urban farming and poor-soil areas

questions.q: Which of these events is an example of the 'untimely rains' that the chapter links with climate change?
o: Heavy rain falls on a ripe wheat crop just before its harvest in spring
The southwest monsoon arrives in June and kharif sowing begins
A farmer irrigates his wheat from a canal in the dry winter months
The northeast monsoon brings rain to Tamil Nadu in November
questions.a: Heavy rain on a ripe wheat crop just before its spring harvest: rain at that time does not fit the season's normal pattern and destroys crops, whereas the monsoons in June and in October-December are their usual timing.

questions.q: Answer these four short parts from the chapter's sections on the role of the government and on landholding. (a) Name three things the government's support system in many states helps farmers to access. (b) The chapter gives 1 hectare = 10,000 square metres and 1 acre = about 4,047 square metres. About how many acres make one hectare? (c) Name the scheme the chapter gives as an example of crop insurance. (d) Why does the government purchase important crops from farmers?
questions.a: (a) Any three of: seeds, fertilisers and pesticides, information on the weather forecast, research and training on new farming practices. (b) 10,000 / 4,047 = about 2.5 acres. (c) The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana. (d) To ensure that farmers have no difficulty marketing their produce and get fair prices.
s: (a) Three of seeds, fertilisers and pesticides, weather information, research and training
(c) Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana
(d) So farmers can market their produce without difficulty and get fair prices

questions.q: A district panchayat in the Ganga basin wants to ease the stress on the river. (a) Of the four causes the chapter gives, which one comes from a worldwide process, and which three come from how people use and control the river's water? (b) Which cause could the panchayat do least about on its own, and which could farmers in the district act on most directly? Give a reason for each. (c) Show, as a chain of links, how the river's stress could reach a family in a city far from the Ganga.
questions.a: (a) Worldwide: global warming melting Himalayan glaciers at an unprecedented rate. From people's use: water diverted to irrigation, groundwater pumped out by agriculture and industry, and hundreds of dams interfering with the natural flow. (b) Least: glacier melt from global warming, because it is a worldwide process no single district controls. Most directly: the water diverted to irrigation or the groundwater pumped out for farming, because these are the farmers' own water use (a reasoned choice between these two is accepted). (c) River under stress -> agriculture in the basin becomes less sustainable -> less food from a basin that feeds over 500 million people -> India's food production is threatened, so food the city family buys becomes scarcer or dearer.
s: (a) Glacier melt from global warming as the worldwide cause; diversion for irrigation, groundwater pumping and dams as the three use causes
(b) Glacier melt as least controllable and irrigation diversion or groundwater pumping as most directly in farmers' hands, each with a reason
(c) A chain from river stress to less sustainable basin farming to threatened food production reaching the city family

questions.q: A state government can fund only one new programme for small farmers this year. Programme A gives every village machines designed for small farms, to rent cheaply. Programme B builds cold storages and gives farmers digital access to market prices and information. (a) Which difficulty of small landholders does Programme A mainly address? (b) Which problem does Programme B mainly address? (c) Name the process the chapter says keeps making landholdings smaller, and say why neither programme can reverse it. (d) Which challenge, called one of the biggest of our time, would neither programme solve? (e) Recommend one programme for a district where nearly every family owns a plot far smaller than the national average, and no one can afford to rent the large tractors that the traders offer. Justify your choice and state one limit of it.
questions.a: (a) Machines such as tractors are designed for larger farms and are expensive to buy or rent, so small landholders find it difficult to use them. (b) Getting better prices for produce: cold storages and better access to information and markets through digital technology help farmers get better prices. (c) Land gets divided among family members over generations; both programmes help farmers work or sell better but do not change how land is inherited, so holdings keep shrinking. (d) Climate change, with untimely rains and more frequent droughts or heavy rainfall that destroy crops. (e) Programme A: the chapter says tractors and other machines are designed for larger farms and are expensive to buy or rent, and that machines have lately been designed for small farms too; renting such machines cheaply answers this district's problem. Limit: it does not stop land being divided further over generations, and small holdings still earn little income.
s: (a) A addresses machines designed for large farms being hard and costly for small landholders to use
(b) B addresses getting better prices through storage and market information
(c) Division of land among family members over generations; neither programme changes inheritance
(d) Climate change, with untimely rains or extreme events destroying crops
(e) Recommends A for the small-plot district with a reason (machines for small farms, cheap to rent) and one limit
